title: {{NAME}} and the Pitch at the Edge of the Wood
moral: The things we make beautiful are worth more than the things we make perfect.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a forest-green and silver soccer jersey, dark shorts, and silver-trimmed cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The pitch at the edge of Whitewater Wood was the worst in the league: sloping, muddy in one corner, with a goalpost that listed slightly to the left.

But it was surrounded by old oaks and a stream ran alongside it, and the wood came right up to the touchline on the east side, and {{NAME}} loved it more than any stadium he'd ever visited.

He was practising alone one evening when the unicorn walked out of the wood and watched him.

He stopped. She didn't leave. He carried on.

pages.content:
She came every evening for a week.

On the eighth day, she walked onto the pitch.

She didn't interfere with the ball. She just stood in various positions and the animals of the wood gradually joined her: rabbits along the east touchline, a badger near one goal, a fox at midfield.

{{NAME}} kept practising and understood, without being told, that the pitch had two audiences: him and all of them.

He started playing for both.

pages.content:
His playing changed.

Not tactically: genuinely. He started making choices based on what was beautiful rather than what was safe. The long ball into space when a short pass was available. The first-time volley when a controlled touch was safer.

Some failed. But the ones that worked had a quality he couldn't name.

The unicorn would make a specific sound on the ones that worked: a low warm note that resonated in the wood's edge.

"You're a critic," he told her.

She made the note again.

pages.content:
He brought his team to practise there.

They were confused at first by the animals and the unicorn.

But within an hour, something had shifted: they were playing for the wood as much as for the league, and the wood was receiving something from them.

The unicorn walked slowly between the groups, her horn catching the last light.

After the session, his teammate said: "I felt different playing here."

"Me too," said {{NAME}}. "Every time."

pages.content:
On the last evening before the league decided to resurface and rebuild the old pitch, {{NAME}} went alone.

The slope, the mud in the corner, the leaning goalpost. The oaks. The stream.

The unicorn came from the wood and stood beside him.

They stood together and looked at it until the light was completely gone.

He went home and in bed he thought: the new pitch will be level and the goals will be straight.

It will be better, probably.

But this was something else.

He fell asleep hearing the stream.
